<objective>
Deliver SERL-02's documented version-deprecation policy and close the phase out against the roadmap's five success criteria.

`.claude/rules/state-serialization.md` already exists and is already the canonical home for serialization rules, but it documents only the bump obligation and has drifted badly: its worked example shows `CURRENT_VERSION` as `'1.0.4'` and a five-entry supported list, when the code carries `'1.0.11'` and twelve entries. It says nothing about which versions are supported in practice, how one is ever retired, what a user sees when an unsupported state is loaded, or — now that plan 02-02 has landed — that a bump also obliges a registry entry.

Purpose: leave the next contributor a policy that is accurate, complete, and impossible to miss.
Output: an expanded, corrected serialization rules document, plus a verified phase close-out.
</objective>

  <action>
First correct the drift. The worked example under "Version Management Requirement" shows `CURRENT_VERSION` as `'1.0.4'` and a five-entry supported list. Update both to match the code exactly: `'1.0.11'` and the twelve entries `1.0.0` through `1.0.11`. A rules file whose example contradicts the source teaches the wrong thing on every read.

Then add a new `## Version Deprecation Policy` section covering four things, each as its own subsection.

Supported versions. State that `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS` in `state-export.service.ts` is the single source of truth, that it currently holds twelve entries from `1.0.0` through `1.0.11`, and that the fixture-coverage guard spec in `state-export.service.spec.ts` fails if a version is added to the constant without a matching fixture. Point at that guard by name so the reader knows the list is mechanically enforced rather than aspirational.

What a bump now requires. Document the full three-part procedure: increment `CURRENT_VERSION`, append the new version to `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`, and append a named entry to the `MIGRATIONS` registry describing the delta. State that even a bump adding only optional fields gets a registry entry whose migrate returns its input unchanged, carrying a comment explaining why no transform is needed — the registry is the record of what changed in each version, and a gap in it is indistinguishable from a forgotten migration. State that a fixture for the new version must be added to the spec's fixture set at the same time.

State also what does *not* require a bump, and record the reasoning as a decision rather than an assertion: a bump is owed when a serialized structure changes — `ExportedState`, `AppState`, `PanelState`, `GlobalSettings`, or any interface in `image-model.interface.ts`. Changes to how already-serialized data is applied on import do not owe a bump. Note that the `1.0.2` to `1.0.3` bump in history did fire for a pure import-behaviour change with no schema delta, that this phase deliberately did not follow that precedent when adding the migration layer and the flip restore, and that structural change is the governing test going forward.

Retirement. Define the process for dropping support for an old version: remove it from `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`, leave its `MIGRATIONS` entries in place because states at newer versions still traverse them, remove its fixture from the spec, and record the removal with its rationale. State the criterion for when retirement is appropriate — no persisted or shared state at that version can plausibly still exist, given that share links are stored server-side and full exports are files a user may keep indefinitely — and state the default posture, which is that no version has been retired to date and retirement should be rare.

Unsupported-version behaviour. Describe exactly what happens today: `validateAndApplyState` throws before any migration or structural check runs, the message names the rejected version, and the four import entry points wrap that into their own error which surfaces to the user through the snackbar or the share-link failure path. State that this is a hard rejection with no partial application — nothing is applied and existing state is left untouched.

Finally add a `## Known Gaps and Scope Decisions` section recording three things a future contributor would otherwise rediscover as surprises. One: fixing the stale dependency-injection mock in `state-export.service.spec.ts` and creating `category.service.spec.ts` were deliberately done in this phase rather than deferred to the later test-coverage phase, because they gate this phase's own regression and refactor work; the later phase's requirements name neither file, so this is a scope call rather than duplication. Two: `indexeddb-user-model.service.ts` still has no spec file — an adjacent coverage gap identified during this phase's research but outside its requirements. Three: the migration registry is intentionally inline in `state-export.service.ts`; if that file passes roughly 700 lines, extract the registry and its walker to a co-located `state-export.migrations.ts` rather than inventing a new directory.

Match the document's existing voice and structure — headed sections, short tables where a table helps, fenced TypeScript only where the existing file already uses it. Keep the front matter untouched.
  </action>
